output.brief: The evidence points mainly at the scholarship change, not the Admissions Office. Yield fell only in the tiers where awards were cut: Dean's from $9k... correction: Dean's fell from $14,000 to $9,000 (yield 45% to 32%) and Merit from $9,000 to $5,000 (45% to 32%). Presidential awards, which were unchanged, and no-award students stayed flat. Early-action decisions went out on time on the old system, yet their yield fell by about the same amount as regular decision (7.4 vs 7.5 points). So slow regular-decision turnaround is not the main driver. Applications and GPA rose, so the applicant pool isn't the cause. The slow turnaround and the portal problems were real and probably cost some individual students, but they don't explain the drop. I am fairly confident (about 80%), though the tier data doesn't split early action from regular decision, and I did not test the missing-transcript claim. Next steps: don't replace the director on this basis. Take the award schedule back to the finance committee with a modelled proposal to restore awards in the Dean's and Merit tiers before award letters go out. Also set a monthly-reported turnaround target for regular decision, and check the portal's document handling before ordering a vendor rebuild.
